newsitem.title: UK: Globalisation marches on despite critics.
newsitem.headline: Globalisation marches on despite critics.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Whether you think it's the way to wealth and opportunity for all or something that will widen the gulf between rich and poor, economic globalisation is here to stay -- and crushing its critics like a giant steamroller.

Last weekend's agreement reached in Geneva to open up much of the world's telecommunications market is the latest example of a trend that began when Soviet-era communism collapsed in 1989, leaving capitalism as the winner.

Driven by super-fast technological changes that have made the world smaller, growing competition and openings in new markets, "globalisation" has become one of the great economic and political forces as the millennium approaches.

Free trade is the aim, with borders increasingly ignored from China to Croatia in the name of money and prosperity. The Geneva-based World Trade Organisation (WTO) watches to see that everyone plays by the rules.

The defenders of globalisation say it creates wealth and jobs, cuts prices and encourages development around the world, breaking cultural boundaries and prejudice, giving a voice to all and even undermining authoritarian governments.

Critics say it destroys cultural diversity in the name of free-market values, lining the pockets of the wealthy industrialised countries while putting the developing world at an ever greater disadvantage, undermining the nation state to boot.
One U.S. commentator has labelled it as an attempt to build "McWorld", a homogenous mass culture, taste-free.
Even in industrial nations, critics say, the pace of change and competition creates unemployment and stress, eroding the values and fabric of society in the name of competition.

Regional deals like the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and European Union's single market are now being supplemented by much wider agreements on everything from telecommunications to agricultural produce.
Business has had to adapt and so have governments.
Diplomats say foreign policy has become increasingly trade-oriented as a result, with far more resources devoted to economic and commercial interests than a decade ago.
For the United States and other Western countries, it has become an essential tool, a way of spreading their values.
The EU's plan to create a single currency by 1999 is partly a response to globalisation, since one currency will make the bloc stronger in competition with the United States and Asia.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, whose country has been a driving force in opening up world markets, hailed the latest telecommunications deal as promising a better future for all.
It would bring "clear benefits to American workers, businesses and consumers alike...and will spread the benefits of a technology revolution to citizens around the world".
A report issued last September by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said business globalisation was increasing at a dramatic pace.
The subject was one of the hot topics at last June's summit meeting of the world's seven leading industrialised nations, the Group of Seven (G7).
The summit hailed it globalisation as an opportunity rather than as a threat, but perhaps the assembled leaders, whose countries account for half the world's trade, had little choice.
Just a few weeks before the G7 summit, World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero said globalisation of the world economy was an unstoppable force.

"Anyone who believes that globalisation can be stoped has to tell us how he would envisage stopping economic and technological progress; this is tantamount to trying to stop the rotation of the earth," he said.

This, however, has not stopped criticism of trade policies and the increasing tendency to deregulate in pursuit of profit -- particularly at recent U.N. summits which have examined how one billion people, or one-fifth of the world's population, languish in poverty and face starvation.

"Many developing countries currently obtain very little (foreign direct investment) and are not as yet a significant part of...global and regional growth strategies. These countries risk being marginalised," last year's UNCTAD report said.
Often, the critics are labour unions or populist politicians in the United States, Europe or Asia, who are trying to place the blame for their country's ills.
Occasionally, though, the criticism comes from unexpected quarters.

Last month, international financier George Soros said that the untrammelled freedom of the market -- which made him a very rich man -- posed a new threat, by making survival of the fittest a leading principle and an ideology out of profit.
"The arch enemy of an open society," he wrote in the U.S. magazine Atlantic Monthly, "is no longer the communist threat but the capitalist one."
